box: Crash/fault tests at every durable transition and concurrent remote edits (milestone 2)
method: Enumerated the journal modules containing fsync or transaction commits, then read the tests that reach each. Test names were not used as evidence; see docs/development.md on why that undercounts here.

rows.note: Kills the process mid-queue and asserts pending, uncertain and acknowledged records each survive in their own state.
SIGKILL between a sealed save and later unsealed writes; the fsynced payload survives verbatim and the newer bytes stay readable.
SIGKILL around a mutation; a pending outcome and an acknowledged receipt both survive.

SIGKILL at both durable transitions. Killed after claim_preparation, the record stays Preparing with no adoptable payload -- a placeholder there would upload an empty replacement over a real document. Killed after complete_preparation, the captured source survives verbatim. Verified discriminating: removing the child's ready signal makes it time out and fail.
Reached only indirectly; no test kills between a generation advance and its commit.

SIGKILL after the handoff and after cleanup. The handoff is durable across the kill and the detached bytes are still on disk when the process dies. What the NEXT journal open does to them is an open question, below.

SIGKILL after the swap and after releasing the reader gate. The swapped name survives -- a crash must not restore the replaced document's name -- the victim stays unlinked, and its bytes remain readable for a descriptor that was already holding them. Verified discriminating.

SIGKILL after the unlink and after the removal mutation is claimed. The name stays hidden even though the remote still reports the file -- a crash must not resurrect a deleted one -- and the removal owed to the cloud is never simply gone. Killing after the claim is the harder case: the mutation is in flight, so recovery cannot assume it never started.
tests/local_directories.rs covers restart; no kill mid-commit.

conclusion: Eight of eleven journal modules carrying durable transitions have a test that kills the process at one. The other three are covered for rollback and restart by injected failure, which is narrower evidence: an injected error unwinds a transaction the program still controls, while a SIGKILL leaves whatever the kernel had actually written. The box says every transition, and seven are not that. It stays unticked.
cheapest_next_step: Generations, directories and publication remain; the pattern is demonstrated eight times over.
not_reachable_autonomously: Physical power loss and a lying fsync are a different class again, need dm-flakey and root, and the milestone text already names physical-fault coverage as an open gap.

open_question_found_while_writing_this.observation: Detached bytes survive the SIGKILL and are gone after the next UploadJournal::open. Measured by checking the spool path before and after reopening: present, then absent.
open_question_found_while_writing_this.why_it_matters: docs/adr/0002-durable-local-edits.md states that detached bytes remain recovery data and that their cleanup and presentation policy is unfinished. A recovery that removes them on the next open is that policy defaulting to deletion, silently. Between a handoff and an explicit cleanup those bytes are the only local copy of an edit whose remote metadata has already moved on.
open_question_found_while_writing_this.not_yet_established: Which recovery step removes them. recover_working iterates working_files, which is empty after a handoff; recover_preparation_files only matches .cirrove-preparing- names. The removal was not located, and it may be correct behaviour rather than a defect.
open_question_found_while_writing_this.why_the_test_does_not_pin_it: Asserting behaviour whose intent is undecided makes a change detector rather than a guard. The test asserts what is settled -- the handoff is durable and the bytes survive the kill -- and this records the rest.
